concepts.name: Magnetic effect of electric current
concepts.description: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it, which can be detected by the deflection of a magnetic compass needle.
concepts.idea: A wire carrying electric current creates a magnetic field around it, which is why it can deflect a compass needle.
concepts.rule: In Activity 4.1, a magnetic compass is placed beneath a wire connected to a cell through a switch. When the switch is moved to ON, current flows through the wire and the compass needle gets deflected from its original direction. When the switch is moved to OFF, the current stops and the needle returns to its original direction. The compass needle is itself a tiny magnet, and this magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials placed in between the wire and the compass. This shows that the current-carrying wire has a magnetic effect on the compass needle: when electric current flows through a conductor such as a wire, it produces a magnetic field around it. This is called the magnetic effect of electric current. The magnetic field disappears as soon as the current stops flowing. The region around a magnet, or around a current-carrying wire, where its magnetic effect can be felt (for example, by the deflection of a compass needle) is called a magnetic field. The magnetic effect of electric current has many practical applications, such as in electromagnets, electric bells, motors, fans and loudspeakers.
concepts.example: When the switch in Activity 4.1 is moved to ON, the compass needle placed under the wire swings away from its resting north-south direction; moving the switch back to OFF lets the needle swing back.

questions.q: Design a simple way, using a cell, a switch, a wire and a compass, to show a friend that electricity and magnetism are connected. Describe your setup and what your friend should observe.
questions.a: Connect a wire to a cell through a switch, and place a magnetic compass beneath the middle part of the wire with the switch OFF; the needle points north-south. Ask the friend to move the switch to ON and watch the needle deflect from its original direction, then move the switch OFF and watch the needle return, showing that current in the wire creates a magnetic effect.

concepts.name: Electromagnets: making one, its poles and its strength
concepts.description: A current-carrying coil behaves as a magnet; an iron core makes it stronger, and it has two poles whose strength and direction depend on the current and the coil.
concepts.idea: A coil of wire carrying current behaves like a magnet; putting an iron core inside makes this electromagnet stronger, and it has two poles like a bar magnet.
concepts.rule: In Activity 4.2, a wire is tightly wrapped around a nail in the form of a coil and connected to a cell (only for a few seconds at a time, since keeping it connected longer weakens the cell quickly). While current flows through the coil, iron paper clips cling to the nail; once the wire is disconnected from the cell, the clips fall off. In Activity 4.3, current is passed through a cylindrical coil of insulated wire and it behaves like a magnet, deflecting the needles of compasses placed near its ends. When an iron nail is inserted inside the coil, the coil becomes a stronger magnet: the deflection of the compass needles is much more, and the coil attracts iron paper clips at its ends. When the current is stopped, the coil loses its magnetic effect. A current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet is called an electromagnet; for practical use, most electromagnets have an iron core to make them stronger. In Activity 4.4, the two ends of the coil (labelled A and B) are tested with a compass one at a time; the end whose pole attracts the north pole of the compass is a south pole, and the two ends of the electromagnet are found to have opposite polarity, so an electromagnet has two poles, North and South, just like a bar magnet. A battery of more cells gives a larger current than a single cell, producing a stronger magnetic field, so the compass needle deflects more and the coil attracts more clips; increasing the number of turns of the coil also makes it a stronger magnet. So the strength of an electromagnet increases with more current (more cells) or more turns of the coil, or both, and its poles reverse if the direction of the current through the coil is reversed.
concepts.example: A cylindrical coil with an iron nail inside it, connected to a battery of two cells, deflects a compass needle more strongly than the same coil connected to a single cell.

questions.q: Explain why an electromagnet, unlike an ordinary bar magnet, can have its poles reversed and its magnetism switched off completely.
questions.a: An electromagnet's magnetism comes entirely from the current flowing through its coil, so its magnetic field exists only while current flows and disappears the moment the current is switched off, unlike a bar magnet which stays magnetic all the time. Reversing the direction of the current through the coil reverses the direction of the magnetic field it produces, which reverses which end becomes the North pole and which becomes the South pole. A bar magnet has fixed poles that cannot be switched off or reversed this way.

questions.q: A friend says 'the only way to make an electromagnet stronger is to add more cells.' Is this complete? Justify your answer.

questions.q: You have a cell, a coil of wire, an iron nail and a compass. Plan a short investigation to find out whether the number of turns of the coil affects how strongly it attracts iron paper clips, and describe what result would support your idea.
questions.a: Wind the coil around the iron nail with a small number of turns, connect it to the cell, and count how many clips it attracts. Then rewind the same wire with a larger number of turns on the same nail, connect it to the same cell, and again count how many clips it attracts. If the coil with more turns attracts more clips than the coil with fewer turns, this supports the idea that more turns make a stronger electromagnet.

concepts.name: Lifting electromagnets and their practical use
concepts.description: Strong electromagnets hung from cranes that a controller switches on to lift iron and steel objects and switches off to release them, used in factories and scrap yards.
concepts.idea: A lifting electromagnet is a strong electromagnet that a crane operator switches on to lift iron or steel objects and switches off to release them.
concepts.rule: Lifting electromagnets are strong electromagnets that can be hung from cranes, instead of a hook, to pick up iron and steel objects; in the introduction story, a nail wrapped with wire and connected to a battery works as a lifting electromagnet, picking up iron paper clips when the circuit is closed and dropping them when the circuit is opened. The crane operator controls the magnet by switching the current ON and OFF: when the current is turned ON, the electromagnet lifts iron or steel objects; when the current is switched OFF, the magnetic field disappears, and the objects are released. This is possible because, unlike a bar magnet, an electromagnet's magnetic effect exists only while current flows through its coil. Lifting electromagnets are widely used in factories and scrap yards to move, lift and sort heavy metal items efficiently. If a lifting electromagnet's circuit is left connected to a cell for too long, the cell can weaken and supply less current; since the strength of an electromagnet depends on the current flowing through it, a weakened cell can make the electromagnet too weak to lift clips or objects any more, even though the coil may still feel warm from whatever small current is still flowing through it.
concepts.example: Sumana's classroom model uses an iron nail wrapped with wire and connected to a battery; closing the circuit lets it pick up iron paper clips like a crane's lifting electromagnet, and opening the circuit drops them.

concepts.name: Heating effect of electric current
concepts.description: Current flowing through a conductor meets resistance, which converts some electrical energy into heat; this heating effect is used in appliances but can also cause overheating problems.
concepts.idea: When current flows through a conductor it meets resistance, and this resistance converts some electrical energy into heat, which is the heating effect of electric current.
concepts.rule: In Activity 4.5, a nichrome wire is connected in a circuit with a cell and a switch. With the switch OFF, the wire feels normal, but after the switch is moved to ON for about 30 seconds and then back to OFF, the wire feels distinctly warm. This happens because, when electric current flows through any conductor, it faces some opposition or resistance to its flow; different conductors offer different levels of resistance, and a nichrome wire offers higher resistance than a copper wire of the same size and length. This resistance converts some of the electrical energy into heat energy, so the conductor gets heated; this warming is called the heating effect of electric current. For the same duration, a battery of two cells heats the wire more than a single cell, because the amount of heat generated depends on the magnitude of the electric current; the heat generated in a wire also depends on the material, thickness and length of the wire, and the duration for which the current flows. In Grade 7 we learnt that an incandescent lamp glows because its filament is heated by an electric current; many household appliances, such as electric room heaters, stoves, kettles, irons, water-heating immersion rods and hair dryers, work on the same principle and contain a rod or coil of wire called a heating element, which can sometimes be seen glowing red hot. The heating effect is useful in these appliances, but it can also cause problems, such as energy loss in wires during transmission and, if appliances overheat, damage to plugs and sockets or even fires; household circuits include safety devices to help prevent such incidents. Because touching a heated wire can cause injury, a nichrome wire that has just carried current should not be touched for an extended period.
concepts.example: Touching a nichrome wire momentarily after current has flowed through it for 30 seconds feels distinctly warmer than touching it before the switch was turned ON.

concepts.name: Voltaic cell: electrodes, electrolyte and chemical generation of electricity
concepts.description: A Voltaic (Galvanic) cell uses a chemical reaction between two different metal electrodes and an electrolyte to generate electricity, as shown by a chain of lemon cells lighting an LED.
concepts.idea: A Voltaic cell generates electricity from a chemical reaction between two different metal electrodes and an electrolyte.
concepts.rule: Cells and batteries are portable sources of electricity. A Voltaic cell, also called a Galvanic cell, contains two metal rods of different materials, called electrodes, partly dipped in a liquid called an electrolyte, which is usually a weak acid or salt solution, placed in a glass or plastic container. A chemical reaction between the electrodes and the electrolyte produces electricity; when the circuit is connected, electric current flows through the external circuit from the positive terminal to the negative terminal. Over time the chemicals inside get used up, and the cell stops working; it is then called 'dead' and cannot supply any more electricity. In Activity 4.6, a copper wire and an iron nail are inserted a little apart into a lemon; the copper wire and iron nail act as the two electrodes, and the lemon juice acts as the electrolyte, conducting electricity between them. Several such lemons are connected together, copper wire to iron nail, in a chain, and an LED is connected between the copper wire of the first lemon and the iron nail of the last lemon. The LED glows, showing that the chain of lemon cells is working as a source of electricity; current can pass through the LED only when its longer, positive terminal is connected to the positive terminal of the cell and its shorter, negative terminal to the negative terminal, so if the LED does not glow at first, reversing its connections should make it glow. A salt solution can also be used as the electrolyte instead of lemon juice.
concepts.example: A chain of five or six lemons, each with a copper wire and an iron nail inserted into it, can light up an LED connected across the ends of the chain.

questions.a: No, not fully. The chapter shows that lemon juice or a salt solution works well as the electrolyte, because they help conduct electricity, but a poor conductor such as pure water would not work nearly as well, so the choice of liquid does matter.

If the LED glows, the cell is working; if it does not glow, reverse the LED's connections and check again before concluding the cell is not producing enough electricity.

concepts.name: Dry cells and rechargeable batteries
concepts.description: Dry cells use a paste electrolyte and are single-use; rechargeable batteries can be charged and reused many times before eventually wearing out.
concepts.idea: A dry cell uses a paste electrolyte and can be used only once, while a rechargeable battery can be charged and reused many times before it wears out.
concepts.rule: Voltaic cells were an important discovery but are not convenient for everyday use, so dry cells are one of the most widely used electric cells today. They are called 'dry' because their electrolyte is not a liquid but a thick, moist paste. A dry cell consists of a zinc container, which acts as the negative terminal, and a carbon rod at the centre, covered with a metal cap, which acts as the positive terminal; the carbon rod is surrounded by the paste-like electrolyte. A dry cell is a single-use cell: once it is used up, it has to be disposed of. Rechargeable batteries, unlike dry cells, can be recharged and reused multiple times, which prevents wastage and saves money over time; they are used for many different applications, from small batteries in watches and phones to larger batteries that power laptops and tablets, and even bigger batteries that run inverters or drive electric vehicles. However, rechargeable batteries do not last forever either: after being charged and used many times, they slowly wear out. As stated in the chapter's own summary, a cell or a battery is a device that generates electric current because of chemical reactions taking place inside it, and rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused multiple times.
concepts.example: A torch uses a disposable dry cell, while a mobile phone uses a rechargeable battery that can be charged again and again until it eventually wears out.

questions.a: An inverter needs to supply a large amount of electricity repeatedly, day after day, so using disposable dry cells would mean constantly buying and replacing a very large number of them, which would be expensive and inconvenient. A rechargeable battery can instead be charged from the mains supply and reused many times over, saving money over time and avoiding the wastage of constantly throwing away used dry cells, even though the rechargeable battery will itself eventually wear out after being charged and used many times.

questions.q: Explain how a dry cell, a rechargeable battery and a Voltaic cell are alike and how they differ, focusing on what generates the electricity in each and how many times each can be used.
questions.a: All three generate electricity through chemical reactions taking place inside them, between their electrodes and their electrolyte. A Voltaic cell typically uses a liquid electrolyte such as a weak acid or salt solution and, like a dry cell, can only be used once before it goes dead, since its chemicals get used up. A dry cell works the same way but uses a thick paste electrolyte instead of a liquid one, making it more convenient to carry, though it is still single-use. A rechargeable battery differs from both in that it can be recharged and reused many times, though it too slowly wears out after being charged and used repeatedly over a long time.

questions.a: Not necessarily. questions.q: A school wants students to compare a dry cell and a rechargeable battery of similar size. Design a simple comparison table with at least three points of difference that the students could fill in, based on this chapter.
questions.a: A comparison table could include: (1) Electrolyte type - a dry cell uses a paste electrolyte, while a rechargeable battery uses a chemical system suited to repeated recharging; (2) Number of uses - a dry cell can be used only once before disposal, while a rechargeable battery can be charged and reused many times; (3) What happens when it runs out - a dry cell must be replaced with a new one, while a rechargeable battery can be plugged in and charged again, until it eventually wears out after many cycles.
